---
title: "Tree rings: divide out the trend"
page-layout: full
format:
  html:
    toc: false
---

This is an application of **detrending**, rather than within-year seasonality: there is one ring-width measurement per year.

Trees differ in their growth levels and slow age-related patterns. We estimate each tree’s trend with a **centered rolling mean**, then divide:

$$I_t=\frac{\text{ring width}_t}{\text{fitted trend}_t}.$$

An index of 1 matches the fitted trend; 0.5 means half its expected width. Compare the same calendar year across trees before and after division. Shared narrow years become easier to see on a common scale.

The stacked view is called a **spaghetti plot** in [dplPy](https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/utilities/#plot). Each tree has its own row: raw widths on the left, detrended indices on the right. All trees share one vertical scale within each panel. Raw curves are centered on their means only for display; their trends and amplitude differences remain visible.

Set **Trees shown** to 1 to inspect any individual tree. **Plot height** enlarges the view; **Curve magnification** controls the vertical zoom. With one tree, its detrended series and the chronology are identical.

The example uses real bristlecone-pine measurements from Campito Mountain, archived by Graybill and LaMarche in [NOAA's International Tree-Ring Data Bank, CA533](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/measurements/northamerica/usa/ca533-noaa.rwl). We take one core from each of 12 tree IDs.

## Try it in Python

[Download the ring widths in mm](ta-data/campito_ring_widths.csv).

The rolling mean averages years within one tree. The chronology averages trees within one year, using a robust mean to reduce the influence of unusual individual values.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

widths = pd.read_csv("campito_ring_widths.csv", index_col="year")
window = 101  # years; try 21, 101, and 301
trend = widths.rolling(window, center=True, min_periods=1).mean()
trend = trend.where(widths.notna())
indices = widths / trend.where(trend > 0)

def robust_mean(year):
    x = year.dropna().to_numpy()
    if len(x) == 0:
        return np.nan
    middle = np.median(x)
    mad = np.median(np.abs(x - middle))
    if mad == 0:
        return middle
    u = (x - middle) / (9 * mad)
    weights = np.where(np.abs(u) < 1, (1 - u**2)**2, 0)
    return np.average(x, weights=weights)

raw = widths.loc[1804:1983].iloc[:, :8]
rwi = indices.loc[raw.index, raw.columns]
chronology = rwi.apply(robust_mean, axis=1)
sample_depth = rwi.notna().sum(axis=1)
offsets = np.arange(len(raw.columns), 0, -1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 8), sharex=True)

for ax, values, title in zip(axes, [raw - raw.mean(), rwi - 1],
                             ["Before: ring width", "After: width / trend"]):
    scale = 0.4 / np.nanmax(np.abs(values.to_numpy()))  # one scale per panel
    for offset, tree in zip(offsets, values.columns):
        ax.axhline(offset, color="0.85", linewidth=0.7)
        ax.plot(values.index, offset + scale * values[tree], linewidth=0.8)
    ax.axvline(1899, color="tab:orange", linestyle="--")
    ax.set(yticks=offsets, yticklabels=values.columns, xlabel="Year", title=title,
           ylim=(-0.6, len(raw.columns) + 0.6))
    ax.text(0, 1.02, f"One row spacing = {1 / scale:.2f} units",
            transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=9)
index_scale = 0.4 / np.nanmax(np.abs((rwi - 1).to_numpy()))
axes[1].axhline(0, color="0.85", linewidth=0.7)
axes[1].plot(chronology.index, index_scale * (chronology - 1),
             color="teal", linewidth=2)
axes[1].set_yticks([*offsets, 0], [*rwi.columns, "Chronology"])
fig.tight_layout()
```

A very flexible trend can remove shared environmental variation along with the age-related pattern. Formal dendrochronology often uses negative exponential curves or splines; this smoother makes that trade-off easy to explore.

The bold row in the after plot is the chronology, using the same index scale as the individual trees. It updates when the displayed trees or rolling-mean window change. We retain the archive's calendar dates; shared narrow years suggest a common influence, not a particular cause.
